ety.text: * Perhaps from चरना (carnā, “to graze, to eat in a crude way”), formed to resemble बरती (bartī), its antonym. * Alternatively, from चरत (carat, “a day not laid down as one for fasting; not observing fast on a day laid down for fasting”) + -ई (-ī). However, चरत (carat) itself is probably a back-formation from चरती (cartī).
Borrowed from Punjabi ਠੁੱਲ੍ਹਾ (ṭhullhā) / ٹھُلّھا (ṭhullhā, “obese”) (compare modern Saraiki ठुल्ला (ṭhullā)); ultimately from Sanskrit स्थूल (sthūla). Doublet of स्थूल (sthūl).

Ultimately derived from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra), with the widespread change in Indo-Aryan descendants qq > g suggesting an intermediary. Cognate with Punjabi ਨਗਾਰਾ (nagārā), ਨਗਾੜਾ (nagāṛā), Nepali नगरा (nagarā), Odia ନାଗରା (nāgarā). Doublet of नक़्क़ारा (naqqārā).

Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀡𑀺𑀢𑁆𑀣𑀭𑀤𑀺 (ṇittharadi, “comes through”), from Sanskrit निस्तरति (nistarati, “it comes forth from, escapes”), from the root निस्तॄ (nistṝ), from तॄ (tṝ), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“to cross over”).

s.g: typical of or befitting a pundit (learned person, Hindu scholar); punditic

ety.text: Hindi verb set बजना (bajnā) बाजना (bājnā) बजाना (bajānā) बजवाना (bajvānā) From earlier बाजना (bājnā), from Prakrit वज्जइ (vajjaï), from Sanskrit वाद्यते (vādyate), the passive form of वादयति (vādayati), from the root वद् (vad, “to speak”). Compare Nepali बज्नु (bajnu), Gujarati વાગવું (vāgvũ), Marathi वाजणे (vāj̈ṇe), Assamese বাজা (baza), Sinhalese වයනවා (wayanawā, “to play (a musical instrument)”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit भूगर्भ (bhūgarbha). By surface analysis, भू- (bhū-) + गर्भ (garbh).
Borrowed from Classical Persian مثل (masal), from Arabic مَثَل (maṯal).

s.g: to load, apply a burden, impose

ety.text: Hindi verb set लादना (lādnā) लदाना (ladānā) लदवाना (ladvānā) Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀮𑀤𑁆𑀤𑁂𑀤𑀺 (laddedi), from Sanskrit लर्दयति (lardayati). Cognate with Punjabi ਲੱਦਣਾ (laddaṇā) / لَدّݨا (laddṇā), Sindhi لَڏَڻُ (laḏaṇu) / लॾणु, Gujarati લાદવું (lādvũ), Marathi लादणे (lādṇe).
Borrowed from Classical Persian شیشه (šīša), from Middle Persian. Cognate with Tamil சீசா (cīcā).

Borrowed from Classical Persian سنجیده (sanjida) (compare سنجیدن (sanjidan, “to ponder, reflect”)), from Proto-Iranian *θanǰáyati, from Proto-Indo-European *t(ʰ)ongʰ-éye-ti, from *t(ʰ)engʰ- (“to draw, pull back”), perhaps an extension of *ten-.
